description: Because I was assigned by my teachers to share my feelings.
summary:
Fire behaves deceptively in microgravity. Without buoyant convection, hot gases do not rise, causing flames to form spherical, slow-burning domes that can smolder undetected. 

To address this danger, we developed Flames in Freefall—an interactive web dashboard for spacecraft fire safety. Grounded in NASA flight investigations (SoFIE, Saffire, and BASS-II), the platform pairs a numerical combustion solver with an interactive 3D flame chamber and a material screening tool. Users can adjust cabin airflow, ambient pressure, and oxygen levels to observe flame spread and extinction limits in real time.

In long-duration space missions, an onboard fire leaves astronauts with nowhere to run. By turning complex microgravity combustion data into an accessible, real-time prediction tool, Flames in Freefall empowers spacecraft designers and life-support engineers to evaluate fire risks, test suppression protocols, and prevent catastrophic disasters before launch.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Fire in space doesn't rise or flicker like on Earth—without gravity, it forms a quiet, dim-blue sphere that standard smoke detectors can easily miss. Even worse, the gentle cabin fans that keep astronauts breathing actually feed fresh oxygen to materials, causing plastics like PMMA to catch fire at just 14.2% oxygen (much easier than on Earth).

We built Flames in Freefall to make this hidden danger visible. By connecting a fast Rust physics engine with an interactive 3D web dashboard, anyone can adjust cabin gravity, oxygen, pressure, and airflow to see how flames behave in real time. The app calculates an instant Fire Risk Score (0–100) and gives clear, step-by-step emergency instructions based on NASA standards.

Why It Matters

Long-duration missions like Artemis (Moon) and future Mars habitats cannot afford trial and error. Our tool helps astronauts and flight designers:

1. Quickly test if cabin materials are safe before launching.

2. Know exactly what to do in an emergency—such as shutting down cabin fans within 3 seconds and using fine nitrogen water mist instead of high-pressure water (which would dangerously splash burning molten plastic across the cabin in zero-g).

Tools & Development

- Physics Engine: Written in Rust for instant mathematical calculations.

- User Interface: Built with Python (Streamlit), WebGL/Three.js for the 3D spherical flame, and Plotly for comparison charts.

- NASA Data & AI: Grounded in real flight data from NASA PSI (SoFIE on the ISS, Saffire on Cygnus, and BASS-II), paired with an offline AI assistant that works even without internet connection.

- Verification: Tested with 406 automated tests to ensure rock-solid stability.

What Makes It Creative

Instead of complex, hours-long supercomputer simulations, we wanted something fast, visual, and accessible. You can drag a slider and immediately watch a terrestrial teardrop flame morph into a microgravity blue dome, giving astronauts an intuitive safety co-pilot right on their tablet.
